content.title: About
content.content: Christophine (also known as black cucumber or African eggplant) is an edible fruit of a tropical plant in the gourd family. When cooked it becomes tender, slightly sweet, and has a soft texture. In cuisine it is commonly used in soups, stews, and braised dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Christophine originates from Africa but is now cultivated in tropical regions of Asia and South America.
The fruit contains a few small seeds that resemble tiny pumpkin seeds.
Unlike common eggplant, christophine has a thicker skin that holds its shape during long cooking.
Traditionally it is featured in curry dishes and Indian "saag" preparations.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked christophine retains a notable amount of vitamin C, which supports immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other gourds, christophine is low in fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolic compounds in christophine may help reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to gourds, including christophine.

items.title: Beware of unripe fruit
items.content: Unripe christophine can contain higher levels of bitter compounds that may irritate the stomach.

items.title: Nutrient interactions
items.content: Large amounts may interfere with the absorption of certain minerals such as iron.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook christophine until tender, then add it to soups, stews, curries, or use it as a filling for pies. It can also be diced and tossed into vegetable salads after cooling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked christophine in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg salad with mayonnaise (1957) is a classic cold dish made from hard‑boiled eggs, mayonnaise, and sometimes additions such as mustard, herbs, or onion. It is popular as a snack, side dish, and sandwich filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first egg‑salad‑with‑mayonnaise recipe appeared in American cookbooks in the late 1950s.
The salad is often served in small portions at holiday tables, especially in the US and Canada.
Variations may include celery, dill, capers, or smoked salmon.
Mayonnaise can be swapped for yogurt or sour cream for a lighter version.
Egg salad is frequently used as a filling for sandwiches, wraps, and stuffed vegetables.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply B12, riboflavin, and folate, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Source of choline
items.content: Choline is important for liver health and cognitive processes.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Mayonnaise made from vegetable oils adds monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps maintain a feeling of fullness longer.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites or yolks.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Mayonnaise makes the salad calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑watching diets.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improperly cooked or stored eggs can harbor Salmonella.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the egg salad chilled as an appetizer, in sandwiches, on lettuce leaves, or as a stuffing for vegetables. Fresh herbs, mustard, or a squeeze of lemon can brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Skim lactose‑free milk is a dairy product from which almost all fat and lactose have been removed. It retains most of the nutrients found in regular cow’s milk, including protein, calcium, vitamin D and B‑vitamins, but is suitable for people with lactose intolerance and those watching their fat intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Skim milk contains about 0.1 % fat, whereas whole milk contains roughly 3.5 %.
Lactose is eliminated by adding the enzyme lactase or by filtration, making the milk safe for most lactose‑intolerant individuals.
Skim milk is a common ingredient in sports nutrition and low‑calorie diets.
Unlike plant‑based alternatives, skim cow’s milk retains the complete animal protein profile.
In many countries it is sold as “0 %” or “fat‑free” milk.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and teeth health and plays a role in muscle contraction and nerve signaling.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Provides about 3.4 g of protein per 100 ml, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D enhances calcium absorption and supports the immune system.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Approximately 35 kcal per 100 ml, making it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Ideal for individuals with lactase deficiency, reducing gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some people may react to casein or whey proteins.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The absence of fat can reduce absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) if not compensated elsewhere.

items.title: Processed product
items.content: Lactose removal often involves enzymatic treatment, which may slightly alter taste.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink it plain, add to cereals, smoothies, coffee, baking recipes, or sauces. It pairs well with fruit, berries, and protein powders.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. Freezing may cause crystallization, so use promptly after thawing.

content.title: About
content.content: Low‑fat milk (1% milkfat) is produced by removing most of the fat from whole milk. It retains the majority of the nutrients found in whole milk, including protein, calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin B12, but provides far fewer calories and saturated fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Low‑fat milk is a common choice in calorie‑controlled diets.
In many countries it is labeled as “1%” or “0.9%” milk.
Milk naturally contains lactose, a sugar that can cause intolerance in some individuals.
Low‑fat milk is quickly absorbed after intense workouts, delivering protein and electrolytes.
Pasteurization preserves most vitamins, but vitamin A is partially lost with the removed fat.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: A 250 ml serving provides about 8 g of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Delivers over 30 % of the daily recommended calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, riboflavin (B2) and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: With only 1 % fat, it helps control calorie intake and saturated fat consumption.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content makes it an excellent beverage for maintaining fluid balance.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People lacking sufficient lactase may experience bloating, diarrhea, and discomfort after drinking milk.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey can cause skin reactions, respiratory symptoms, or anaphylaxis.

items.title: Vitamin A content
items.content: Because most fat is removed, vitamin A levels are lower than in whole milk; prolonged exclusive use may require an additional source.

items.title: Processing additives
items.content: Some brands add stabilizers or sweeteners; check the ingredient list if you prefer a clean product.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Low‑fat milk works well with cereals, in smoothies, for sauces, baking, and as a base for protein shakes. It can be enjoyed cold or gently warmed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 1–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑taste.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato sauce and meat is a home recipe that combines whole‑grain pasta, a flavorful tomato‑based sauce, and tender meat. The dish offers a balanced mix of complex carbohydrates, protein, and beneficial vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than regular white pasta.
Tomato sauce made from fresh tomatoes is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
Tomatoes retain a high amount of vitamin C when the sauce is not overcooked.
Lean beef or turkey is commonly used, reducing saturated fat content.
Homemade sauce lets you control salt and sugar levels, making the meal healthier.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta supplies dietary fiber that aids digestion and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Meat adds complete protein necessary for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes in the sauce contain lycopene, which may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the whole grain pasta and meat provide B1, B3, and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron from meat and magnesium from whole grains, important for blood formation and nerve function.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should use a gluten‑free alternative.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce can be salty; monitor added salt to keep sodium intake moderate.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Using fatty cuts of meat can increase saturated fat; opt for lean cuts whenever possible.

items.title: Acidity of tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes may aggravate acid reflux in some people; reduce sauce amount if needed.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Cook whole grain pasta until al dente. Sauté finely chopped meat until browned, then add onion, garlic, and tomatoes; simmer 15‑20 minutes, seasoning with basil, oregano, salt, and pepper. Toss the pasta with the sauce, serve hot, and optionally garnish with grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared pasta in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze for up to 2 months after cooling, using freezer‑safe bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Sugar substitute and sugar blend (5016) is a combination of natural and artificial sweeteners designed to lower the calorie content and glycemic index of foods without losing sweet taste. The blend is suitable for baking, beverages and desserts, providing stable sweetness and texture comparable to regular sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend contains low‑calorie sweeteners (e.g., erythritol) together with a small portion of regular sugar to improve flavor.
The sweeteners do not cause dental caries and have minimal impact on blood sugar levels.
The blend has been tested for thermal stability and retains sweetness at temperatures up to 200 °C, making it suitable for baking.
The product is certified gluten‑free and allergen‑free according to international standards.

items.title: Reduced Calorie Intake
items.content: The blend provides up to 70 % fewer calories than regular sugar, helping to control overall energy balance.

items.title: Low Glycemic Index
items.content: Low‑GI sweeteners reduce rapid spikes in blood glucose, beneficial for pre‑diabetic and diabetic individuals.

items.title: Caries‑Free
items.content: Artificial sweeteners do not promote tooth decay, making the product safe for dental health.

items.title: Supports Food Texture
items.content: A small amount of sugar in the blend helps maintain the structure of baked goods, preventing crystallisation and dryness.

items.title: Individual Intolerance
items.content: Some people may react to artificial sweeteners (e.g., diacetyl). Discontinue use if discomfort occurs.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Although reduced, the product still contains a minor amount of sugar, which should be considered in strict sugar‑free diets.

items.title: Gut Microflora Impact
items.content: High doses of certain sweeteners (e.g., sorbitol) can cause gas and diarrhea.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: The blend can be used in the same proportions as regular sugar for baking, desserts, sauces and drinks. When cooking at high temperatures, adding a small amount of regular sugar can improve caramelisation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed container. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated to prevent moisture absorption and clumping.
